title: Summer Refinement Series, Part 2: Making Learning Stick with Cornell KOs
author: Sol in the Wild
summary: This is the second installment in Sol's Summer Refinement Series, focused on what happens after new knowledge is introduced: how to help students retain, retrieve, and apply it long after teaching ends. The author identifies the 'illusion of learning' -- students who perform well on assessments but forget quickly afterward -- as a design problem rather than a motivation problem. The proposed solution is Cornell-style Knowledge Organizers (Cornell KOs), which structure notes around key questions that double as built-in retrieval practice tools. Unlike passive note-taking, Cornell KOs enable students to leave class with a self-quizzing tool already prepared. The article explains how Cornell KOs complement FASE (a structured read-aloud routine) by pairing FASE's attentional benefits with retrieval's retention benefits. Together, the two routines create a bridge from initial learning to long-term retention through nightly homework, daily Do Nows, and scheduled spaced retrieval sessions. The piece sits within a broader argument that 'what we call a motivation problem is often a design problem,' and that systematic routines -- not incidental review -- are the true mechanism of durable knowledge.
points: The 'illusion of learning' -- students pass assessments but forget quickly -- is a design failure of the instructional system, not a motivational deficit; building retrieval practice into classroom structure addresses the root cause.

Cornell KOs work because each note page is organized around key questions, so students leave class with a built-in retrieval-practice tool ready for self-quizzing -- not just a passive record of content.

Research shows retrieval practice (recalling information from memory) is more effective for durable learning than re-reading or passive review; Cornell KOs bake this mechanism directly into the note-taking structure.

FASE reading (structured read-aloud with random cold-calling) addresses the attention bottleneck before information can enter working memory; Cornell KOs address the retention bottleneck that follows.
Spaced retrieval across homework, Do Nows, and scheduled sessions compounds initial learning into genuinely durable long-term retention, rather than short-lived test performance.
quotes: One of the most frustrating experiences in teaching is watching students perform well on an assessment only to struggle to recall the same information a few weeks later. For years, I viewed this as a motivation problem. Increasingly, I see it as a design problem.

Research consistently shows that retrieving information from memory strengthens learning more effectively than simply rereading or reviewing notes. The act of recalling information is not merely a way of measuring learning. It is one of the most effective ways of creating it.
By organizing notes around questions, students leave class with a built-in retrieval practice tool already prepared.

As cognitive science has shown, students cannot learn information they are not attending to. Before information can be stored in long-term memory, it must first be processed in working memory and only what we pay attention to will enter working memory.

FASE reading helps students attend to and process new information during instruction. Cornell KOs help students retrieve and strengthen that information after instruction. Together, they create a bridge between initial learning and long-term retention.

Rather than treating reading and taking notes as a one-time event, students repeatedly revisit and retrieve the knowledge gained from those readings through nightly homework, daily Do Nows, and scheduled spaced retrieval sessions.
